turns.prompt: A least-recently-used (LRU) cache with a fixed capacity is often built from a hash map plus a doubly linked list of entries ordered by last use. What does each part contribute? Walk through what happens on a cache hit for key k, and explain why both get and put can run in O(1) time on average.
turns.answer: The hash map is used just to store the values while the doubly linked list holds the keys in the order they were inserted, and on a hit we simply replace the value in the map and move the whole list one step forward; because we never have to search the list, both get and put end up being constant‑time operations.

follow_ups.answer: The hash map gives us a quick way to find the value for a key, and the linked list just records the order in which items were added so we can walk it to the front on a hit; because we only ever touch the head or tail of the list and never scan through it, both get and put end up being constant‑time operations.
